desc:
You have two separate undirected trees. The first has edges1.length + 1 nodes numbered from 0, the second has edges2.length + 1 nodes, also numbered from 0. Each list contains the edges [a, b] of its tree (an empty list means a tree with a single node).

You must add exactly one new edge that connects one node of the first tree with one node of the second tree, producing one big tree. You may choose the two endpoints freely. The diameter of a tree is the number of edges on its longest path. Return the smallest diameter the combined tree can have.

edges1 = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]]        (a star, diameter 2)
edges2 = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3]]        (a path of 4 nodes, diameter 3)

join the star's center to a middle node of the path   -> 4
constraints: Both lists describe trees (connected, no cycles) on nodes numbered 0..edges.length
The two trees use separate node numbering; nodes of the two trees never need to be compared
hints: Whatever you do, the new diameter is at least as large as the diameter of each tree on its own.

A new longest path may cross the new edge: it goes from one tree to the other. It is shortest when the edge joins the two trees at their centers, because a center minimizes the farthest distance inside its tree.

Let d1 and d2 be the two diameters. The farthest distance from a center of a tree with diameter d is ceil(d / 2). The answer is max(d1, d2, ceil(d1/2) + ceil(d2/2) + 1); find d1 and d2 with the two-BFS method.
editorial: Let d1 and d2 be the diameters of the two trees. After joining, the old longest paths still exist, so the result is at least max(d1, d2). In addition there are paths that cross the new edge (a, b): the longest one has length ecc1(a) + 1 + ecc2(b), where ecc is the farthest distance from a node to any node of its own tree.

To minimize it choose a and b with the smallest eccentricity in their trees, namely the centers. The smallest eccentricity (the radius) of a tree with diameter d is ceil(d / 2). So the best crossing path has length ceil(d1/2) + ceil(d2/2) + 1, and the final diameter is the maximum of this and the two original diameters.
Computing d1 and d2 takes two BFS runs per tree, so O(n1 + n2) time and space overall. A single-node tree has diameter 0 and radius 0, which the formula handles without special cases.
